summary: Specifies ways to configure DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) clients with their DOTS servers, including for the signal channel Call Home. Knowing the right server for a location helps a client ask for attack mitigation, even when it cannot tell where the attack is coming from.

eli5.summary: When your network is under attack, you need to know whom to call for help. This explains how devices automatically find the right helper.

questions: how does a dots client find its server
what are the dhcp options for dots
which port does the dots signal channel use
subtitle: How a DDoS signaling client finds the server to ask for help, using DHCP, DNS records or DNS service discovery.

tldr.problem: A DOTS client under attack needs to know which DOTS server to contact, and no single way of learning that fits every network. The same question applies in reverse for signal channel Call Home.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a priority order: explicit configuration (local or DHCP), then S-NAPTR service resolution, then DNS-based service discovery. It adds DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options and new DNS service tags.
tldr.outcome: Clients get a consistent, operator-friendly way to find servers, with the same logic reused to find Call Home clients. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 8973 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. IANA assigned the DHCP option codes, the service names and the S-NAPTR tags described above.

sections.title: The Discovery Problem
sections.content:
DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) lets a DOTS client tell a DOTS server that its network is under attack and that mitigation is needed. The signal channel carries mitigation requests, and the data channel lets clients install named filtering rules. A DOTS agent is any DOTS-aware module that takes part in a channel.

RFC 8973 specifies how a client discovers its server. The same methods let a server locate a client for signal channel Call Home, where the roles are reversed. The RFC assumes the credentials to authenticate DOTS servers are already provisioned to the client. Picking among servers for multihomed clients is out of scope.
sections.eli5: If a house is on fire, you must know the fire station's number before the fire. This RFC is about how a device learns that number by itself.

sections.title: Why Several Mechanisms
sections.content:
The RFC argues that one discovery method cannot suit every deployment. Many use cases involve customer premises equipment (CPE), for which DHCP or service resolution are natural. DHCP can also tie a DOTS server name to the DNS servers that can resolve it, and can hand out addresses directly and avoid lookup delay. S-NAPTR lookups let server administrators publish a preferred transport protocol. When the upstream network provider is not the DDoS mitigation provider, the server name is expected to come from the service subscription, that is, manual configuration.

The result is a unified logic that combines DHCP, S-NAPTR resource records in the DNS, and DNS Service Discovery.
sections.eli5: Different houses find the fire station in different ways: a card on the fridge, the phone book, or asking a neighbor. So the RFC allows several ways.

sections.title: The Discovery Procedure
sections.content:
All DOTS clients MUST support at least one of three mechanisms and SHOULD implement all three, or as many as practical. Clients prefer them in this order: (1) explicit configuration, which is either local/manual configuration or automatic configuration such as DHCP; (2) service resolution; (3) DNS-SD. A fixed priority matters because operators otherwise end up hunting for devices that picked the wrong server.

On hosts with several interfaces or address families, discovery runs for each interface and address family combination. Discovery happens when the agent starts and is repeated when a validity timer (such as a DHCP lease or DNS TTL) expires, when the peer's certificate expires, or on attachment to a new network. The same procedure is followed by a Call Home DOTS server to find its Call Home client.
sections.eli5: Check the fridge card first, then the phone book, then ask a neighbor. Do it again if the card runs out or you move to a new house.

sections.title: DHCP Options
sections.content:
DHCP can supply two things: the name of the peer DOTS agent (a reference identifier used to authenticate its certificate, or a name to resolve) and a list of its addresses. DHCPv6 uses OPTION_V6_DOTS_RI (141) and OPTION_V6_DOTS_ADDRESS (142). DHCPv4 uses OPTION_V4_DOTS_RI (147) and OPTION_V4_DOTS_ADDRESS (148). Addresses are listed in order of preference. The DHCPv6 address option length MUST be a multiple of 16, and the DHCPv4 one is 4*N for N addresses; for DHCPv4, RFC 3396 MUST be used if it exceeds 255 octets.

Client rules: use only the first instance of an option received, and silently discard multicast and loopback addresses. If both name and addresses arrive, the name is used only as the reference identifier and MUST NOT be passed to a resolver; the addresses are used to connect. If only a name arrives, it is resolved and also used as the reference identifier. If only addresses arrive, they are used to connect and can serve as identifiers.
sections.eli5: DHCP can hand over a name tag and a list of phone numbers. If you get both, you dial the numbers and use the name tag only to check you reached the right place.

sections.title: Service Resolution with S-NAPTR
sections.content:
First the agent learns a DNS domain for each interface and address family, for example from DHCP. Then it makes S-NAPTR lookups (RFC 3958) with an application service tag and an application protocol tag. The RFC defines the service tags DOTS and DOTS-CALL-HOME, and the protocol tags signal.udp, signal.tcp and data.tcp. The chain of NAPTR records leads to SRV records and finally to addresses.

In the worked example for example.net, the result in order is UDP signal at 2001:db8::1 port 5000, TCP signal at the same address port 5001, TCP data at that address port 5002, and TCP data at 2001:db8::2 port 443. With default ports, discovery returns 4646 for the signal channel and 443 for the data channel. If no DOTS-specific S-NAPTR records are found, discovery fails for that domain, and a client MUST wait an appropriate time before retrying a failed lookup.
sections.eli5: The phone book entry does not give the number right away. It points to another page, which points to another, until you reach the actual number and which door to knock on.

sections.title: DNS Service Discovery
sections.content:
DNS-based Service Discovery (DNS-SD, RFC 6763) names a service instance as <Instance>.<Service>.<Domain>. For DOTS the service part MUST be one of _dots-signal._udp, _dots-signal._tcp, _dots-data._tcp, _dots-call-home._udp or _dots-call-home._tcp. This document defines no TXT keys, so the TXT record is empty.

The RFC's example lists two UDP signal channel servers, a and b, both with the same priority and port 4646, each announced through a PTR record and described with an SRV record.
sections.eli5: Instead of one fixed list, the network posts a sign for each kind of service, and your device reads the sign that says "DOTS help here."

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
DOTS agents must authenticate each other with (D)TLS before a session is valid. An attacker who blocks DHCP can push a client down to a lower-priority mechanism, so the risk is that of the fallback method. Contacting a discovered server over an interface it is not bound to can add delay and reveal that DOTS is enabled and who the provider is.

With DHCP, an active attacker could spoof responses that point to an attacker-run DOTS agent holding a domain-validated certificate. A mitigation is a preconfigured list of trusted DOTS domain names, checked against the DNS-ID in the server certificate. For service resolution the main attack is impersonating the peer by compromising S-NAPTR resolution; DNSSEC data validated that way is proven authoritative. For DNS-SD, DNSSEC SHOULD be used where authenticity matters, and secure DNS updates SHOULD generally be used to control who may change records.
sections.eli5: A trickster could swap the number on the fridge card for his own. So the device keeps a list of names it trusts and checks the helper's ID badge.

viz.caption: DISCOVERY MECHANISMS IN ORDER OF PREFERENCE

items.title: 1. Explicit configuration
items.text: Local or manual configuration, or automatic configuration such as DHCP.

items.title: 2. Service resolution
items.text: S-NAPTR lookups that lead to SRV records and addresses.

items.title: 3. DNS-SD
items.text: DNS-based Service Discovery using the _dots-* service names.

viz.caption: DHCP OPTION CODES ASSIGNED BY RFC 8973

items.label: OPTION_V6_DOTS_RI
items.desc: DHCPv6: FQDN of the peer DOTS agent, used as reference identifier.

items.label: OPTION_V6_DOTS_ADDRESS
items.desc: DHCPv6: one or more IPv6 addresses, in order of preference.

items.label: OPTION_V4_DOTS_RI
items.desc: DHCPv4: domain name of the peer DOTS agent.

items.label: OPTION_V4_DOTS_ADDRESS
items.desc: DHCPv4: one or more IPv4 addresses, in order of preference.
